activity: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
knowledge_domain: argument structures, nuanced reasoning and conditional thinking in abstract and hypothetical discussion
fact: A counterfactual conditional describes what would have been true if things had been different, such as 'if Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it', and usually implies the 'if' part is false.
story:
The bus pulled away from the curb at 7:41, and Aidan reached the stop at 7:44, which meant he was still carrying his debate notes when he jogged through the side door of the school twenty minutes later, sweating through his shirt. The regional semifinal was fourth period. He had left his partner's copy of the affirmative case in his locker, and his partner, Walid, was already in Mr. Whitaker's room setting up the podium markers.

"If I'd left five minutes earlier," Aidan said, dropping into the chair beside him, "I would have caught it. If I'd caught it, I'd have been here by eight, and we'd have run the rebuttal drill twice."

Walid didn't look up from the cards he was sorting. "You keep saying that. Five minutes earlier, this, that. You can't check any of it. It's like arguing about a world that doesn't exist."

"It's not a world, it's a sentence. It's reasoning."

"It's torture," Walid said, but he smiled, and dealt the cards like a dealer who knew the game was fixed anyway.

Mr. Whitaker, who coached the team and taught the logic elective nobody else wanted, wandered over with his coffee. He had a way of standing at the edge of a conversation until you pulled him in. "What's torture?"

"Aidan missed the bus and now he lives in the past," Walid said.

"There's a name for that kind of sentence," Mr. Whitaker said. "If he'd left earlier, he would have caught it. A counterfactual conditional." He tapped Aidan's notes once with one finger. "The 'if' part is false, and everyone knows it, and we say it anyway. Look it up if you want the full picture." Then he went back to his desk, which was how he ended every conversation, as if the last word were a stone he'd tossed into a pond for you to fish out yourself.

Aidan wrote it on the back of a flow pad while Walid ran the rebuttal drill alone: counterfactual conditional, if part false, "If Sally owned a donkey, she would ride it," which was the example in the encyclopedia entry he found on his phone under the desk. He liked the donkey. It was so plainly hypothetical, so cheerfully unowned, that it made his bus seem ridiculous by comparison. At the same time he could feel the difference between the two sentences, though it took him a while to name it. The donkey sentence was empty, a machine with nothing inside it. His sentence had a weight, because something real was sitting on the false side of the "if": a semifinal, a partner who had drilled alone, a case he had half written and half copied from a forum at two in the morning.

The case itself was about secularism, and this was the part that had been eating at him all week. The resolution asked whether states should retire religious law from their constitutions. Walid's family had come from a country where a clerical court had once fined his uncle over a complaint about a noxious smell from his bakery oven, a fine everyone knew was really about the family's sect. Walid argued the affirmative the way a person walks out of a building on fire. Aidan had built the negative, the defense of accommodation, because someone had to, and because Gary kept needling him in the cafeteria that abandoning the negative would be intellectual surrender.

"You can't just emancipate yourself from the hardest side of the question," Gary had said on Tuesday, gesturing with his fries. "That's not winning the argument, that's quitting it."

"That's easy for you to say," Walid had answered. "You've never lived in a theocracy."

Aidan had sat between them saying nothing, and the nothing had followed him to the bus stop and onto the bus he missed and into Mr. Whitaker's room. Now, watching Walid run the drill with sharp, economical gestures, Aidan understood that he had been doing with his own argument what he had done with the bus. He kept asking what the case would look like if he had better evidence, more time, a different resolution, and the answer was always beautiful and always checkable by no one. The donkey sentence. A world that didn't exist.

So he crossed out three of his four contentions during lunch and rebuilt the fourth on something he could actually defend: not that religious establishment was good, but that a state that abolished it overnight, without institutions to replace the functions it served, would leave people like Walid's uncle with fines from a different court for the same bakery oven. It was a conditional of a more honest kind, and it might be wrong, and he could live with that in a way he couldn't live with the donkey.

In the semifinal, Walid attacked the rebuilt contention hard, cross-examining him for the full three minutes, and Aidan conceded one point, held two, and lost the round on speaker points by a margin so thin the judge apologized for it. Afterward, in the corridor with the water fountains that tasted like pennies, Gary said the rebuild was the best thing Aidan had ever run, and Walid said the cross-examination had been better, and both of them were right.

"You still think about the bus?" Walid asked on the way to the bus loop.

"I think about it accurately now," Aidan said. "If I'd left five minutes earlier, I'd have caught it. And I can't ever check that, which means I should probably stop using it as evidence."

"Progress," Walid said, and shoved him toward the door of the 4:10. "Get on this one."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: The World Health Organization recommends adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day, which is less than 5 grams of salt, to help lower blood pressure.
story:
The blood pressure cuff hissed like a tire losing patience, and Holly sat very still on the picnic bench with her arm through the loop, watching the needle the way people watch a kettle they don't trust. "Higher," she said. "No, lower. What's it doing?"

"Nothing yet," Anthony said. "It's inflating. Stop being a difficult patient."

"You're the one who volunteered for the junior health aide track," Marie-Eve said from the other side of the table, where she was sketching the cuff's dial into her notebook for reasons she refused to explain. "We're just the bodies."

The junior health aide track was Anthony's idea, formed sometime in week two of camp, when the infirmary cabin had seemed cooler than the canoe dock and considerably cooler than the volleyball milieu, where he had distinguished himself mainly by getting hit in the face twice in one afternoon. Ms. Park, the camp nurse, had agreed to teach him one thing properly: how to take a blood pressure reading, and how to explain what changes it. At the end of the month she would test him. If he passed, he'd be allowed to take readings for real during the camp's family visiting day, sitting at a small table with a poster he'd made himself.

The mechanical part came quickly. Wrap the cuff, find the pulse at the wrist, inflate until the needle stopped jumping, then ease the pressure down and listen for the first knock and the last one. Holly's was 112 over 70, which he announced with such ceremony that she stood up and bowed. Marie-Eve made him do it twice to be sure, and got 108 over 66, and demanded a prize.

The explaining part was harder. Ms. Park had given him a stack of pamphlets and one instruction: "Don't memorize. Understand it well enough to say it to somebody's grandmother." That was the sentence he kept chewing on during free swim, floating on his back near the roped-off shallow end, because grandmothers were exactly the population of family visiting day, and grandmothers, in his limited experience, asked follow-up questions.

The sodium lesson came to him sideways. Ms. Park's infirmary had a shelf of canned soup for the days when a camper needed something bland, and one rainy Wednesday, waiting out the storm under her tin roof, Anthony picked up a can and turned it over. "Four hundred and eighty milligrams of sodium," he read. "Per serving. That's a lot, right?"

"Depends what you're measuring against," Ms. Park said, and went back to her inventory.

He measured against the pamphlet himself, thumbing through until he found it: the World Health Organization recommended adults eat less than 2 grams of sodium a day to help lower blood pressure, which was less than 5 grams of salt. He sat with the can in his lap and did the arithmetic twice. Two cans of soup, if a person ate both servings, would put someone nearly halfway to the whole day's limit before lunch. His own grandmother, he remembered, kept a cupboard of exactly these soups, and ate them with saltines, and had once told a doctor who asked about her diet that she "never salted anything," which had seemed, at the time, like a solid defense. He had never known what a day's limit looked like. Now it looked like a shelf.

"Ms. Park," he said, "how is it that soup companies get away with this?"

"They don't salt it for fun," she said. "Well. Not only for fun." She took the can from him, looked at the label, and set it back with the label facing out, like a librarian reshelving a troublemaker.

By the last week of August he was ready, or as ready as readiness got in his estimation, which was to say he had rehearsed his explanation on Holly until she could recite it back in a mocking falsetto, and on Marie-Eve, who had made him translate it into terms she called "human." The human version went: the reading is pressure in the pipes, exercise over time tends to bring it down, sodium pushes it up, and the limit is under 2 grams of sodium a day, less than 5 grams of salt, and yes, that is smaller than it sounds, and no, your soup is not your friend. He'd made the poster with a drawing of a soup can wearing a villain's mustache, which he privately considered his finest work and publicly attributed to Marie-Eve.

Assessment day arrived with the visiting-day crowd. Ms. Park set him up at the small table, and his first real patient was Holly's father, then two aunts, then a small queue of grandmothers, each of whom wanted her number spoken loudly and each of whom argued with it. He took six readings, explained the salt thing four times, and felt a spreading, slightly embarrassing altruistic glow, the kind that made him understand why people became nurses instead of, say, accountants.

Then Ms. Park sat down across from him at the quiet end of the hour and held out her own arm. "One more," she said. "Practitioner's privilege." He wrapped the cuff, inflated it, and watched the needle as the pressure dropped. One-forty-eight over ninety-four. He let the air out slowly, checked the dial, checked it again, and looked up. Ms. Park was looking past him at the infirmary shelf, where the soup cans stood in their bright, salty row, labels out.

"Ms. Park," Anthony said carefully, "how many servings would you say you have in a week?"

She took the cuff off her arm, folded it, and patted it like a dog that had behaved.

"Why don't you fix me a poster," she said, "something with a mustache on it."

activity: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
knowledge_domain: to read a short news article in a new language and summarise it aloud
fact: English newspaper headlines often drop small words like 'the' and use the present tense for past events, a compressed style sometimes called 'headlinese'.
story:
Hayden commandeered the wicker chair by the lobby window before his father could claim it, because the light there was good and the free newspapers were stacked three feet away. The family had been in the city six days, long enough that his mother had stopped translating prices aloud and his sister had stopped complaining about the bread, and long enough that Hayden had begun the project he'd promised Ms. Levy he would continue abroad: read one short news article in the language of the country, then summarize it aloud. Except that the hotel's complimentary papers were mostly in English, aimed at tourists and expats, which felt like cheating until he found, tucked inside one of them, a thin weekly section printed bilingually, English on the left page and the local language on the right, the same articles twice.

Kabir found him there an hour later, still on the first page. Kabir was the desk clerk's son, seventeen like Hayden, and had appointed himself Hayward's guide on the grounds that anyone who ordered coffee by pointing at the menu deserved help. He dropped into the opposite chair and helped himself to Hayden's pastry without asking, which by now was a settled custom between them.

"Today's article is about a bridge," Hayden said. He turned the paper so Kabir could see. "Small one, one column, there's a photo of a man in a hard hat looking upset. I can read the right-hand page okay, mostly, I looked up maybe nine words. But the English side is the problem, and I grew up speaking English, so that's embarrassing."

Kabir read the headline out loud, slowly, as if tasting it. "Minister Defends Bridge Delay." Then he read it again, and his face did the thing it did when he was working on a puzzle, the eyebrows gathering toward the middle. "This sentence has no grammar at all. Who is defending? When? There is a minister, there is a defense, there is a delay, and then it simply stops."

"It doesn't stop, it's a headline," Hayden said, and then stopped himself, because Kabir's confusion had opened a door in his own head and he could see he'd never actually walked through it. He had read headlines all his life the way he breathed, without once asking how. "Hold on. Say the sentence normally. As a whole sentence."

"The minister defends the delay of the bridge," Kabir said. "Present tense. But the article says the minister defended it yesterday. Yesterday, in a press conference, past. So the headline is wrong, or the headline is doing something."

Hayden took out his notebook, the one with his word lists and the numbers of bus routes he'd ridden, and wrote the headline at the top of a fresh page. Under it he wrote what was missing: the. Just the. He looked at the bilingual page again, the local-language version of the same title, and it had all its small words, every one, sitting there like buttons on a shirt. "They drop the small words," he said. "The, a, is, and instead of defended they just say defends. And we all understand it anyway. We've been trained by every newspaper we've ever seen."

"Trained to read broken sentences and call them normal," Kabir said, delighted. "Is there a name for this illness?"

Hayden didn't know, and said so, and Kabir, who had a phone with better reception than anyone in the building, searched for a moment and then held up the screen. "Headlinese," he read. "It is called headlinese." He pronounced it carefully, twice, and Hayden wrote it down with a small star beside it, the mark he used for words he wanted to keep.

They went through the rest of the section together, which was how the morning got lost. Kabir's father came by once with coffee, frowned at the two of them bent over a newspaper like reactionary old men in a café, and shook his head at the state of the world. Kabir ignored him. He read headlines aloud as if reciting poetry in a language with no verbs: "Council Rejects Taxi Plan. Ferry Strike Ends. Mayor Urges Calm." Each time he untangled it, supplied the missing the, moved the verb back into the past where it belonged, and each time Hayden checked the local-language side to see whether it had done the same trick. It never had. The right-hand page always kept its grammar, complete and unhurried, and he found himself wondering which version was really the compressed one, the English with its gaps you had to fill, or the other with everything present but somehow slower.

At the end, Hayden did the thing he'd been avoiding all morning. He closed the notebook, turned to the local-language article about the bridge, and summarized it aloud, haltingly, in that language, for Kabir to hear: a delayed bridge, a minister defending it, a cost that had grown, a town that was unhappy. His verbs came out in the wrong tenses and Kabir corrected two of them, gently, and Hayden noticed that his own sentences, in his new language, sounded a little like headlinese themselves, dropping words he didn't yet have, leaning on the present because the past felt risky. Whether that made his version wrong or merely compressed, or whether those were even different things, he couldn't yet say. Kabir pushed the last piece of pastry across the table toward him and pointed at the ferry strike headline. "That one next," he said. "It has good verbs."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Children accounted for about one-third of food bank visits in Canada in March 2025, according to Food Banks Canada's HungerCount report.
story:
Mason arrived at the community garden at eight, half an hour before anyone else, because his mother had said showing up early was the only impression that mattered and he had decided, on the walk over, that he was allowed to disagree with her about that and still do it. The food bank shared the lot with the garden: three raised beds of kale and late tomatoes behind a chain-link fence, and a low cinderblock building where the hampers got packed on Saturdays. He signed his name on the clipboard hanging by the door and stood there holding the pen until Devyn came in carrying a crate of juice boxes and said, "You can put the pen down. It's not a hostage."

Mr. Wiśniewski, who ran the garden and, apparently, the food bank too, put Mason on the hamper line with Devyn and Lawrence. The work was simple and repetitive, which Mason had not expected to like. Each family got a numbered slip; you read the number of people and built the box from the shelves: rice or pasta, cans of beans, powdered milk, and then the shelf at the end, the one Devyn supervised like a customs officer, with baby formula and jars of puréed fruit and sleeves of crackers shaped like fish. Mason noticed, by the tenth hamper, that almost every slip included something from that shelf. He kept counting without meaning to.

"You're doing the face," Devyn said. Lawrence laughed without looking up from his taping.

"What face?"

"The one where you're about to say something about the system. Don't. Just pack."

"I'm not saying anything about the system. I'm just noticing how many have kids' stuff in them. Like, way more than I would've guessed." He set a jar of pear purée into box fourteen and slid it down the table. "Is that normal?"

Devyn pulled a folded printout from the back pocket of her apron, the way other people carried a phone, and smoothed it on the table between the cans. "HungerCount," she said. "It's the survey Food Banks Canada does. Children were about one-third of food bank visits in this country in March 2025." She said it flatly, the way you'd read a bus schedule. "So yeah. Normal."

Mason thought about the figure while he packed, and the thinking interfered with his hands, so that he put the crackers in a box marked for a single adult and had to take them back out. A third of the visits. He had come here with two ideas already in his head and had not realized they were two ideas until they collided over box sixteen. The first was his mother's, which was that charity was how decent people covered for themselves, a way to commodify other people's hunger into a receipt you could feel good about. The second was Lawrence's, apparently, which Lawrence stated while taping: "People need food, we have food, that's the whole equation." Both positions felt true and neither felt sufficient, and Mason understood that standing between shelves of powdered milk was not the place to resolve it, and also that it was exactly the place, because the boxes kept coming either way.

Mr. Wiśniewski came through at eleven with a basket of tomatoes from the garden, the small ugly ones, and set them on the end table for anyone who wanted them. "Volunteers take some too," he said. Mason watched Lawrence take four and put them in his backpack, which was ordinary, and then watched Lawrence take the hamper slip for family number twenty-two, his own handwriting suddenly careful and slow on the label, and carry the box out to the back where the bikes were. Nobody said anything. Devyn looked at the floor. Mason understood, in one rearranging moment, that the line he had been standing on all morning ran straight through the building, through the clipboard, through his own signature at the top of it.

He thought about his mother's word for this, complicity, about how she used it like a verdict. He thought about how Lawrence had been packing boxes for other families all morning before packing his own. He could not make the two facts sit still next to each other. Maybe the whole arrangement was pernicious, quietly rotting things from underneath, and maybe it was just a Saturday, imperfect and necessary, and the honest position was to hold both and keep handing cans down the table. He did not know. He noticed that not knowing did not stop his hands.

Box twenty-three went to a woman with a boy asleep against her shoulder, and Mason put in an extra sleeve of the fish crackers because Devyn had turned away to sneeze and the chance was simply there. She thanked him and did not smile, and the boy's shoe had come half off, and they walked to the parking lot through the smell of tomato vines.

"You want the last of the pears?" Devyn held up the jar from box fourteen, the one he'd pulled the crackers from and never corrected.

"Give it to twenty-two's box," Mason said. "There's room."

Devyn looked at him for a second, then walked it out back, toward the bikes.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passes with no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults.
story:
Olivier backed the car between Ms. Korhonen's recycling bins and a row of cardboard boxes she had weighted with sand, the garage door rattling half open above them like a flag. The boxes were the curb. He had touched them four times already, and each time Misha, playing the examiner from a folding chair with a clipboard he had brought from his dad's office, had made a small tick in the air with his pen.

"Fault," Misha said now, for the fifth time, in the flat voice he used when he was enjoying something and pretending not to.

"That's not fair, you didn't even look at the wheel." Olivier kept his hands at ten and two, the way the instructor had drilled into him, though the car was in park and the engine was only idling. "You're just ticking things."

"I'm being realistic. Examiners aren't going to pathologize every little thing, but they're not going to miss the curb either."

From the workbench, where she was sorting screws into jars she could no longer see well enough to label, Ms. Korhonen said, "In my day the examiner wore gloves and wrote nothing down at all. You passed or you didn't, and then you drove him to the bank, because he'd been meaning to go." She was the reason they had the garage at all; she had offered it the day she watched Olivier's dad coning off the actual street and nearly causing a scene with the neighbours.

Rishi was sitting cross-legged on the cold concrete with his phone, because Rishi actually read things. "Here," he said. "It's not one mistake and you're out. On the practical test you can pass with up to fifteen driving faults." He looked up. "Fifteen. But no serious faults and no dangerous faults. Those fail you straight away."

"Fifteen," Olivier repeated. He let go of the wheel and leaned back against the seat, which still smelled of the pine air freshener his mother insisted on. He had been driving for two weeks as though the whole exam were a single wrong inch, as though the curb were a cliff. On Thursday, his actual test, he had touched the curb once during the parallel park, felt the wheel ride up and then off, and had spent the rest of the route certain he had failed, so certain that he had stopped checking his mirrors properly, which, he understood only later, was the kind of thing that actually failed people.

"So that's fifteen," Misha said, ticking the air again. "You used five in one afternoon on boxes."

Olivier got out of the car and stood looking at the gap between the bins and the boxes. Here were the two ideas he had been carrying around and could not make sit together. One was his father's, delivered over dinner: drive like a surgeon operates, because a car is a machine that kills people and there is no small error. The other was Rishi's fact, this strange arithmetic of forgiveness, fifteen chances built into the system itself. He had assumed the second was soft, that a test that let you make fifteen mistakes was a test that didn't take driving seriously. But standing in the cold garage, he could see it another way: that the fifteen faults and the one dangerous fault were the same idea expressed twice. The exam didn't say mistakes don't matter. It said that almost all mistakes, the ordinary human ones, accumulate, and that only the ones that could actually hurt someone end you immediately. That was stricter than his father's version, not softer. His father treated every error as fatal; the test treated the truly fatal ones as fatal and refused to pretend the rest were.

"The thing I don't know," he said slowly, "is where the line is. On Thursday, when I touched the curb, was that a driving fault, or was it serious? It's not like they announce it."

"Maybe they do it on purpose," Rishi said. "Make it uncertain so you drive carefully the whole time, even after you mess up. Because if you knew you'd failed, you'd just stop trying, and then you'd drive badly, and they'd have a bad driver on the road thinking they had nothing left to lose."

"That's the most words you've said all day," Misha said.

"I read the forums."

Olivier turned back to the car. He had been planning, all week, to treat his rescheduled test as a debt to be paid perfectly, an austerity. He changed his mind standing there, or began to. Not to be blase about it, not to drive like Misha, who had failed once already and described it with a shrug that made Olivier's chest hurt on his behalf. Something between: to drive as though the curb mattered, and to know, if he touched it anyway, that a single touch was one fault out of fifteen, and that the correct response was not to fall apart but to keep checking his mirrors for the rest of the route. He could not make himself certain about which side of the line his Thursday mistake had fallen on, and he decided, in a way that felt like putting down something heavy, that he did not have to resolve it tonight.

"Okay," he said, and got back in, and adjusted the mirror, and put both hands at ten and two. "Bin, box, bin. Sit there and be the examiner again, but this time say what kind of fault it is. Make me argue with you."

Misha picked up the clipboard. "Driving fault," he said. "Failure to wait."

Olivier checked over his shoulder, signalled, and started backing in.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: Hydroplaning happens when a layer of water builds up between the tires and the road so the car loses traction; easing off the accelerator can let the tires regain grip.
story:
Keira had been amortizing this lesson in her head for weeks: forty dollars an hour, spread across the money she'd made bagging groceries, until the number was small enough to ignore. Then the rain came, which felt like the universe charging interest. The driving school's hatchback sat in her driveway with its passenger-side mirrors plastered in drops, and beside it stood Ms. Papadopoulos, her former physics teacher, wearing a rain hat that made her look like a small determined mushroom.

"You're early," Ms. Papadopoulos said, tapping the roof. "Good. Get in, check your mirrors, and remember that the driver's seat is not a suggestion."

The roads out past town were country roads, the kind that went from tar to gravel to something friable at the shoulders, all loose stone and crumbling edge. Keira drove them the way she did everything at seventeen, which is to say carefully, with a running commentary she couldn't turn off. "Ten and two. No, nine and three. Which one is it?" Ms. Papadopoulos said either worked and asked her, pleasantly, to stop narrating her own hands.

The rain thickened as they left the last houses behind. Fields went silver, then went away. Keira had the wipers on fast enough to hypnotize a small animal. She was beginning to think the whole outing might be uneventful, and she was almost disappointed, because uneventful meant she'd spent months of grocery money to steer in a straight line.

Last summer, before any of this, Hala had taught her to drive a riding mower in Tom's grandmother's field, shouting instructions over the engine. "Slower, you're mowing the fence!" Hala had yelled, and Keira had laughed so hard she nearly went into the pond. Tom had filmed the whole thing and titled it "entropy in action," because the field always ended up messier than they started. It had felt like freedom, that mower. The hatchback felt like a test she hadn't studied for.

From the passenger seat, Ms. Papadopoulos watched the road and the girl in almost equal measure. She had taught physics for nineteen years and had learned that the students who talked too much were usually the ones thinking too much, and that both conditions improved with practice. She also watched the standing water ahead, a long shallow sheet stretched across a dip in the road, and she did not say anything about it, because she believed you could tell a student a thing a hundred times or you could let the road tell them once.

The front tires hit the water and the steering went light under Keira's hands. Light like the wheel had been unplugged. The car drifted, small and slow and enormous all at once, toward the crumbling shoulder. Her foot went for the brake and something, some leftover instinct from the mower or from Hala shouting slower, said no. She eased off the accelerator instead, just took her foot away and held the wheel loose, and for a second that lasted a season nothing happened, and then the tires bit the road again, ordinary and solid, and the car was hers.

"Hydroplaning," Ms. Papadopoulos said.

"That was it? That's the thing from the videos?" Keira's voice came out an octave up. "The water gets between the tires and the road and you just, lose it, you're floating?" She was laughing now, the shaky kind. "And you let off the gas and it comes back. That actually works. I thought that was a myth like the ten and two thing."

"Ten and two has never been a myth, it's been a preference," Ms. Papadopoulos said. "There's a difference, though I'll concede the textbooks have been unreliable lately." She pointed ahead to a wide gravel pull-off. "Take us in there. We're going to do it again."

"We're going to what now?"

"Back and forth through that dip. Gently. If the road is going to teach you, we might as well amortize the lesson." Ms. Papadopoulos settled back into her seat and pulled a thermos from the door pocket. "Twice more and I'll share the tea."

Keira turned the car around at the pull-off, gravel popping under the tires, and headed back toward the silver sheet of water sitting in the dip. She set her hands at nine and three, took a breath, and eased down on the accelerator.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
knowledge_domain: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data
fact: Guessing a whole number from 1 to 100 by always picking the middle of the remaining range never takes more than seven guesses, which is binary search in game form.
story:
Kevin's grandfather had beaten him at chess twice that afternoon, which the old man attributed to "fifty extra years of watching people make mistakes," and so Kevin, sulking only slightly, proposed a different contest. "Pick a number from one to a hundred," he said. "I'll guess it. Higher or lower."

His grandfather agreed, leaning back in the kitchen chair with the confidence of a man who had survived three recessions and one regrettable haircut in 1974. "Sixty-two? Is it higher or lower?" Kevin began.

"Higher."

"Eighty-one."

"Lower."

"Seventy-two. Higher or lower?" Kevin asked, tapping the table between them. The old man's eyebrows began a slow migration toward each other.

"Lower."

"Sixty-seven."

"Lower."

"Sixty-four," Kevin said, and watched his grandfather's mouth tighten. "Lower. Sixty-three. Higher?" A reluctant nod. "It's sixty-two." He hadn't started at sixty-two; he'd arrived at it, closing from both sides like a door.

"That's not guessing," his grandfather protested, dealing himself a fig newton as consolation. "That's interrogation."

"It's seven questions maximum," Kevin said, crumbs of pride in his voice. "If you always take the middle of what's left, you never need more than seven guesses for one to a hundred. Sixty-two was the midpoint of everything you hadn't ruled out. That's all I did." His grandfather demanded proof, so they played four more rounds. The old man lost all four, once in five guesses, once in a full seven, and after the last one he said, "You'd better not explain this to your grandmother, or she'll refuse to play cards with either of us," which Kevin took as high praise.

The next evening he sat cross-legged on his bedroom floor with his laptop, the house quiet except for the dishwasher's low rumble downstairs. Ms. Gagnon had posted the assignment that morning: implement a search on a sorted array, and write a short justification for the approach you chose. The textbook chapter kept insisting that a linear search, walking through the numbers one at a time like a man checking every house on the street, was "simpler." Kevin found this annoying in a way he couldn't quite defend. Simpler for whom? For the programmer, maybe, on a Tuesday, with ten numbers. Not for the numbers.

He typed until midnight anyway, breaking it twice, once by telling the computer the wrong direction and once by asking the computer to guess the same wrong number seven times in a row with the serene patience of a machine that trusts you completely. Around eleven Leo texted him a photograph of his own screen, on which the word "ERROR" appeared in a font Leo had somehow made larger, and beneath it: "is the computer allowed to just lie to you like this." Kevin wrote back, "it's not lying, you are," and then, feeling circumspect about his own glass house, did not send the follow-up joke. Instead he sent: "pick the middle. always the middle. like the number game." Leo replied with a single thumbs-up, which in their shared language meant either "understood" or "goodbye forever," and Kevin went back to work.

By the time his mother knocked on the door to tell him the lights were for sleeping, the code ran. He tested it with the same game his grandfather had lost: a sorted list, a hidden value, a loop that halved the world with every question. Seven was the ceiling; often it was fewer. He wrote the paragraph for Ms. Gagnon, deleted a sentence that began "Obviously," because Emma had once told him that a person who writes "obviously" is about to pontificate, and he refused on principle to become that person before college. Then he rewrote the paragraph three times, and each time it got shorter and truer. What he could not get rid of was the small honest knot at the center of it: the approach only worked because the data was already sorted, and sorting had its own cost, and which cost mattered more depended on how many searches you planned to do, which the assignment hadn't said. He left that part in. It felt like admitting the floor was load-bearing.

The next morning Emma read the paragraph over his shoulder in the kitchen while she waited for the toaster, a ritual she performed with the entitlement of someone who had known him since the fourth grade. "You called yourself an egoist in the third draft," she said. "Why did you cut that?"

"Because it wasn't true. I just liked the sentence."

"The sentence was funny. That's not the same as true, but it's worth something." She handed him half a piece of toast, which in their economy was a peace treaty. "What are you going to say when Gagnon asks you to explain it out loud?"

"The number game," Kevin said. "Everyone's played it. You pick a number between one and a hundred, and if you take the middle every time, you can't lose. It's called binary search, and grandpa can verify it experimentally, at cost to his ego."

His grandfather, passing through with the crossword, paused at the doorway. "That's my legacy, is it. Being defeated in front of my own wife."

"You lost in five guesses once," Kevin said. "Nobody's calling you bad at this."

"I want a rematch," his grandfather said, and pulled out a chair. "And this time, Emma picks the number."

activity: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
knowledge_domain: to explain how a central bank raising interest rates slows inflation
fact: The Taylor rule, proposed by economist John Taylor, says that when inflation rises one percentage point a central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point.
story:
Angelina had spread her notebook across the kitchen table the way her mother spread laundry, and for the same reason: everything had to be visible at once or it would go missing. In three weeks she would be in a dormitory four states away, and the economics club she had joined for the college application and stayed with out of stubbornness was meeting tonight, the last meeting, at her end of a video call because the school building was already closed for the summer.

They were arguing about inflation again. Reed, whose camera was off as always, said what he had said at every meeting since spring, that if inflation went up by one percentage point the central bank should just raise its interest rate by one point too, keep the scales balanced, done.

"You match it," he said. "That's the whole move."

"That's not the whole move," Angelica said, from her bedroom with the tapestry behind her. "But I can't say why it isn't."

Angelina muted herself, looked at her mother washing lettuce at the sink, and unmuted. "Can I try something? I looked this up yesterday because you two have been fighting about it since March and I got tired of listening." She had gotten tired of listening on Tuesday, walking home past Ms. Siddiqui's garden, and had spent that evening with her laptop on this same table, taking notes she now couldn't fully read.

"Go ahead," Reed said.

"There's a thing called the Taylor rule," she said, and the name felt strange in her mouth, like using a stranger's first name. "When inflation rises one percentage point, the central bank should raise its interest rate by more than one percentage point. More. Not equal."

"Whose rule?" Angelica asked.

"An economist named John Taylor proposed it," Angelina said. "That's all I've got. I found the rule and I found the name and I have been sitting here since yesterday trying to figure out why more is different from equal."

Ms. Siddiqui, who had come over to drop off tomatoes and stayed for the argument because she claimed central banks were the only gossip worth following, lowered herself into the chair across from Angelina. "Don't look at me. I sell houses. I only know what the rate does to my buyers."

Angelina pulled the notebook closer and read her own handwriting aloud: matching means standing still; going further means moving against. "Okay, so here's where I got to. If you only match it, you're keeping pace with something that's already running. You're not catching it. You have to go further than it goes." She stopped, because she could hear herself starting to sound like the textbook she'd abandoned, the one that had explained nothing and eulogized economics instead, praising its elegance for three chapters before showing her a single graph she could use.

"Say the inflation part again," Reed said, camera still off.

"One point up in inflation, more than one point up in the rate. That's the rule."

"So I was wrong," Reed said. He said it flatly, the way he said most things, and Angelina, who had spent the spring with a somewhat jaundiced view of Reed's confidence, waited for the rest of it. It came, quietly. "I liked matching better. It was fair. One for one."

"It was fair," Angelina agreed. "That might be why it's wrong. Fair isn't the same as effective." She said it and then heard how much she was claiming, and pulled back. "Except I still can't tell you the difference between fair and effective in an actual economy with actual people in it. I can tell you the rule. I can't tell you why the rule works, or whether it always works, or who it hurts when it does."

"Then say all of that," Angelica said. "At the meeting. That's a better position than the one you had in March, which was falling asleep on camera."

The three of them laughed, and Angelina's mother set a bowl of tomatoes on the table without comment, and Angelina wrote one more line in the notebook, the last line she would write in this kitchen: more than one for one, and I don't know the rest yet. This final week at home had a strange weightlessness to it, the pure liminality of it, no longer a high school student, not yet a college one, and she had been afraid it would be all drift. It turned out you could learn one true sentence and hold onto it like a rail.

"Motion to end the meeting," Reed said.

"Seconded," said Angelica, and Angelina, unmuted now and grinning at a screen that held one dark square and one bright one, closed her notebook and carried it, with the tomatoes, to the counter where her mother stood.

activity: getting a first part-time job
knowledge_domain: getting a first part-time job
fact: Most US employment is at-will, meaning the employer or the worker can end the job at any time for any reason that is not illegal.
story:
The application asked for two references, and Andrew put down his mother and a man he had never worked for. The hardware store sat at the end of Main Street between a laundromat and a shuttered nail salon, and its owner, Mr. Yang, read the application upside down for a full four seconds before turning it right side up, which Andrew chose to interpret as a test of composure rather than eyesight. Mr. Yang asked whether he could lift forty pounds, whether he knew the difference between a lag bolt and a carriage bolt, and whether he had ever stolen anything, in that order, and Andrew answered yes, mostly, and no, in that order. He was hired on a Tuesday.

The work was straightforward until it wasn't. Andrew restocked bins of washers whose sizes had drifted into each other over the years, swept aisles, and learned that customers who said "I just need a quick thing" would take an hour. On his fourth shift Mr. Yang had him price a shipment of paintbrushes, and Andrew discovered that the previous shipment had been priced wrong for three weeks, which meant either the system was off or somebody before him had been careless. He thought about the somebody before him a lot. Nobody had mentioned a previous employee. There was a coffee mug in the break room with a chip in the rim that nobody used.

Andy came in on Saturday to buy sandpaper for his father and lingered by the register. "You like it?" he asked, in the tone of someone hoping the answer was no, so that his own job bagging groceries could remain the group's agreed-upon tragedy. Andrew said it was fine, honestly fine, and found he meant it, which unsettled him more than hating it would have. The exhilaration of a first paycheck was still recent enough that he could hold the envelope up to the light like a slide. Andy said his manager scheduled him for closings without asking, and then Andy said the thing that rearranged Andrew's week: "I'm just going to stop showing up. You don't legally have to stay, right? It's not like a contract."

Andrew did not know. This was the part that bothered him, that he had signed things at orientation without reading them, that he had taken the word of a boy who once insisted that the moon landing had been filmed in Nevada. At home he looked it up, and the answer arrived plainly, without ceremony. Most employment in the United States is at-will, which means the employer or the worker can end the job at any time, for any reason that is not illegal. He read it twice. It worked both directions, like a door with hinges on neither side in particular.

He remembered, then, the woman who had trained him for one shift before vanishing. She had shown him where the keyed duplicates hung and said the mop was in the back and that was all, and when he asked Mr. Yang where she had gone, Mr. Yang had said, "Elsewhere," and continued shelving. Andrew had filed the moment away as one of the small oddities of adult life. Now he contextualized it differently: she had used the same door Andy was describing, the one that swings out as easily as in, and Mr. Yang had not seemed wounded, only brief.

He tried to bring both ideas together and found they resisted each other like the mixed bins of washers. On Monday he asked Mr. Yang, while they sorted hex nuts, whether he was supposed to give notice if he ever quit. Mr. Yang did not look up. "Supposed by whom?" Andrew said he didn't know, maybe the law. "At-will," Mr. Yang said, and dropped a nut into its bin with a click. "You can go when you like. I can let you go when I like." He said it the way a man reports the weather, and then he added, "But I write references for people who give two weeks, and I write them well." That was the whole speech. Andrew nodded and sorted.

He understood, roughly, that there were two kinds of freedom here and they were stacked on top of each other. The legal one was clean and absolute and meant nothing about consequences. The other one, the two weeks, the chipped mug, the "Elsewhere," was unwritten and probably mattered more and could not be looked up anywhere. Andy's plan suddenly looked less like rebellion and more like a coin spent without checking its value. Andrew still wasn't sure he would stay at the store through the fall, or whether honesty required him to decide now rather than later, or whether deciding not to decide was itself a decision. He put the last hex nut in its bin and carried the empty box toward the back, where the mop was, still, in the back.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1966 experiment by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward; this is called the pratfall effect.
story:
Gabriel arrived at the stadium gate twenty minutes early, which he knew was its own kind of tell, and stood in the ticket line rehearsing a single sentence he had decided not to say. The sentence concerned coffee. Specifically, it concerned a study from 1966 by Elliot Aronson and colleagues, in which a highly competent quiz contestant who spilled a cup of coffee was rated more likable afterward, a finding Gabriel had read three days ago and had been carrying around since like a coin he was afraid to spend.

Zoey arrived at seven sharp, wearing the school's colors as a joke, a scarf so enormous it was practically a second student. "I brought hot chocolate," she said, holding up two paper cups from the gas station across the road. "One of them is for you, if you want to owe me a favor forever."

They found seats on the aluminum bleachers at the forty-yard line, where Damien was already installed with a bag of sunflower seeds and an unshakable opinion about the offensive line. Gabriel had known Damien since fifth grade, and Damien had a way of absorbing every silence into commentary, which tonight Gabriel found himself both grateful for and quietly resenting. When Zoey laughed at something Damien said about the referee's posture, Gabriel felt the evening tilt toward a night among friends, which was safer than what he had actually asked her for when he'd said, two weeks ago, leaning against a locker, "Do you want to go to the game? Not with everyone. Just us."

On the third play of the second quarter, a boy two rows down lunged for a passed chip, struck Zoey's elbow, and sent her hot chocolate over Gabriel's sleeve and onto his jeans. It was hot enough that he stood without deciding to. Zoey's face did the thing faces do when someone believes they have ruined something irreversibly: the quick flat apology, the hands hovering, the retreat into a smallness that was nothing like her. "I'm so sorry. This is, god, this is the whole evening, I've soaked you."

"It's fine," Gabriel said, and heard how little that carried, and watched her start building the wall that people build when they're sure the night is over. Behind them Damien called out something generous and useless about laundering. Gabriel sat back down, wet and sticky and suddenly very calm, because the coin was finally in his hand and there was nowhere to hide it.

"You know there was this experiment," he said. "1966, Elliot Aronson and some colleagues. People watched a quiz contestant who was really good, like clearly competent. One version of him spills a cup of coffee during it. And afterward people rated the coffee-spiller more likable."

Zoey looked at him with the particular attention she gave things she couldn't decide were strange or brilliant. "More likable for spilling coffee."

"That's the finding. It's called the pratfall effect." He could hear his own voice, a little too even, a student delivering a fact he wanted to be true. He pushed through it anyway. "So you haven't ruined anything. If anything, my jeans just did you a favor."

She laughed then, a real one, and pressed her napkins against his knee without ceremony, and for a while the game went on beneath them, the crowd rising and falling, Damien's seeds cracking like small applause. Gabriel let himself believe the fact had worked, that the spill had been converted into something.

But by the fourth quarter he was less sure, and he tried to be honest with himself about it, the way his mother had once told him perspicacious people were supposed to be. Maybe the study was true and also not the whole truth. Maybe Zoey had softened not because he'd cited an experiment but because he'd bothered to, because he'd offered her something awkward and sincere when she expected to be dismissed. Or maybe those were the same thing, the citation and the kindness, and he couldn't separate them, and didn't need to. He had wanted a rule he could rely on, some mechanism that would absolve the evening of its clumsiness, and what he had instead was a girl who had moved a foot closer on the cold bench and was now explaining, in a low voice, why she thought the band's halftime show had been secretly about divorce.

After the game, in the parking lot crowds, Damien peeled off toward the buses with a lifted fist and a peroration about next week's opponents that nobody waited to hear the end of. Zoey turned to Gabriel under the stadium lights, the scarf now around both of them at her insistence, though the excuse she offered was that he looked cold. "So," she said. "Same experiment. If I trip getting to the car, do I get even more likable, or is there a limit?"

"I don't think they tested the limit."

"Then we'd better find out," she said, and stepped off the curb deliberately wrong.

activity: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
knowledge_domain: the idea that scientific consensus forms through repeated studies, peer review and replication rather than one result
fact: The Higgs boson discovery on July 4, 2012 was announced only after two separate CERN detector teams, ATLAS and CMS, independently found the same new particle.
story:
Hadi's message arrived at 9:40 on a Tuesday, which was how most of their arguments began. "Look at this," he wrote, and pasted a link to an article with a headline claiming that a single new study had proven phones were destroying teenagers' attention spans. "Told you. My mom's going to use this on me tonight."

Kayla leaned closer to the screen, chewing the end of a pen. She and Hadi had been fighting about screen time for a week, ever since her own mother had read the same headline aloud at dinner with an air of triumph. If Hadi's mother joined the campaign, Kayla's cause was lost on two fronts. She typed back, "One study doesn't prove anything," and then, because that sounded like something a person says when they're losing, she deleted it.

"One study," she sent instead, "is one study." Then she opened a new tab, because a feeling wasn't going to win this. She needed ammunition.

The problem was that she didn't entirely know what she was looking for. She knew studies got checked, somehow, but the checking felt like a locked room adults kept the key to. She typed "how do we know science is right" and got a mess of philosophy forums, then tried "how are big discoveries confirmed," and somewhere in the third page of results she landed on a page about the Higgs boson. She'd heard the name in physics class, the way you hear about a celebrity you'll never meet. What caught her was a detail buried in the middle of the article: the discovery had been announced on July 4, 2012, only after two separate teams at CERN, called ATLAS and CMS, had each independently found the same new particle. Two enormous detectors, built side by side, staffed by scientists who weren't allowed to peek at each other's numbers until the end.

She read it twice. She'd assumed, without ever thinking about it, that big discoveries arrived like lightning, one flash and everyone believed. Instead it was more like two witnesses who hadn't compared notes describing the same suspect. One team could fool itself. Two teams, working separately, landing on the same answer, that was harder to argue with. It wasn't proof like in geometry class. It was agreement, earned the slow way, study after study, other people trying and failing to break it.

Downstairs, her phone buzzed. Hadi again: "My mom already showed me the article twice. She's printing it. She's literally printing it." Kayla laughed, then stopped laughing, because she recognized the maneuver. His mother wasn't equivocating, she was legislating.

"Come over," she typed. "Bring your laptop."

He arrived twenty minutes later, nonchalant in the way of someone who claims not to care while carrying a printed article in his backpack like evidence for trial. He flopped onto her desk chair and nodded at her screen, where she'd left the CERN page open.

"Physics homework?" he said. "This is about phones."

"It's about how we know things," she said. She spun the chair so he faced the monitor, her hand on the backrest, and told him what she'd found. Two detectors, ATLAS and CMS, separate teams, same particle, and only then the announcement on July 4, 2012. "Nobody stood up and said, we found it, believe us. Two groups had to find the same thing on their own first."

Hadi squinted at the page. "So the phone study is, what, half an experiment?"

"It's one result. Until somebody else runs it and gets the same answer, it's a maybe with good publicity."

He pulled the printed article from his backpack and laid it on the desk between them, smoothing the crease. Kayla watched him read his mother's weapon with new eyes. He wanted to be right, she understood suddenly, but he also wanted a truce at his own dinner table, some way to hand his mother an argument she could respect instead of a slammed door. She felt the same pull at hers.

"So I show her this," he said slowly, tapping the CERN page, "and say, if it's real, it'll survive being repeated. If it doesn't get repeated, then we wait."

"And if it does get repeated," Kayla said, "I'll hand my mom the phone myself." She heard herself make the promise and let it stand, even though part of her wasn't sure she'd keep it, even though the study might turn out to be right and she'd lose the whole war in front of her. That was the uncomfortable part: the method she liked didn't guarantee her side won. It only guaranteed somebody honest ended up right.

They sat without talking for a minute, the cursor blinking on the page. Downstairs her mother called something about snacks.

"Detente," Hadi said, testing the word like a coin he'd just learned the weight of.

"Until the next headline," Kayla said. She took the printed article from the desk, folded it in half, and slid it under her keyboard for safekeeping.

activity: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
knowledge_domain: professional tone, structured writing and respectful disagreement in formal communication
fact: Paul Graham's 2008 essay 'How to Disagree' ranks disagreement in seven levels, from name-calling at the bottom to refuting the other person's central point at the top.
story:
The group chat had forty-one unread messages by the time Tristan sat down at his internship desk, and the argument was already on fire. It had started over the summer volunteer event at the community garden, which Ziad wanted moved to Saturday and Graeme insisted had to stay Sunday, and within eleven messages someone had called someone else "a parasite with a phone plan." Tristan scrolled upward, watching reasonable sentences dissolve into caps lock, while Ms. Farah's printer extruded page after page of meeting minutes behind him, slow and orderly, as if mocking the entire chat.

He was supposed to be drafting a client email. He had been shown the house style that morning: a subject line that said what the email was about, a first paragraph that stated the request, and a closing that thanked the reader for their time, not for their "understanding," which Ms. Farah had crossed out on his practice draft with a pencil she kept for exactly that purpose. "If you want understanding," she'd said, "call your mother." He'd laughed, then realized she hadn't. Now he typed and deleted three openings, and behind him his phone buzzed again. Graeme had moved on to questioning Ziad's GPA.

"Tristan. Focus," Ms. Farah said, without turning from her filing.

"One second." He was searching something. He remembered Ziad mentioning it a week ago, offhand, in the way Ziad mentioned things, like tossing a coin onto a table. Paul Graham's 2008 essay "How to Disagree." It ranked disagreement in seven levels, from name-calling at the bottom to refuting the other person's central point at the top. Tristan read it twice on the office computer, cheeks warm, because the chat was a perfect specimen of the bottom of the ladder. He copied the link. Then, because the house style had soaked into him without his noticing, he structured his reply: no insults, no sarcasm, a clear statement of the problem, and, at the end, a direct question to Graeme. Graeme's central point, near as Tristan could find it, was that Sunday was the only day the garden coordinator could supervise. Was that true, or was it the assumption everyone had inherited from March? The chat went quiet for six minutes, which in group-chat time was a geological era.

In those six minutes, Ziad stood at the counter of the hardware store where he worked Saturdays, phones prohibited, cutting window screen from a roll for a woman who kept changing her mind. He wanted, more than he had admitted to anyone, to be the one who ran the volunteer event this year. Not for the résumé, though the résumé was real; he wanted it because his brother had run it before him and had graduated, and the event felt like something that could be lost. When he'd texted "Saturday" that morning, he had been arguing for a day, but underneath that he had been arguing for himself, and Graeme's reply, "you just want to be in charge," had landed somewhere precise. That was why the insult had come back. He rolled another foot of screen and thought about that, the complicity of it, how the fight had only ever been partly about the calendar. On his break he checked his phone and found Tristan's message, the link, and the question. He read the essay standing between the paint mixer and the exit, and the word that stayed with him was "levels." Seven of them, and everything he'd typed that morning had been at the bottom.

He typed back: "Coordinator can do either day. I asked her. That's a fact, and it's higher than what I said before." Then, after a pause: "I do want to run it. Fine. Say that to my face." Graeme replied within a minute, which meant he'd been holding his phone the whole time. "You should run it. You're the only one of us who's ever read an email all the way through."

Tristan's client email went out at 4:40, four paragraphs, no adverbs, a closing that thanked the reader for her time. Ms. Farah read it over his shoulder in the way of someone inspecting a wall they suspect of being load-bearing. "Better," she said. He waited. "You used 'sagacious' in the third paragraph." He had. He pointed out that the client had used it first, in her original request, and Ms. Farah considered this, then said, "Then it's her word. Borrowed tools still build the shed," and initialled the printout.

That night the chat agreed on Sunday, and on Ziad running the event, and on a rule that anyone typing in capitals had to wait ten minutes before sending. Graeme proposed the rule himself, which surprised no one who knew him, because Graeme's central point had never really been the day of the week. Tristan watched the plan take shape, messages stacking cleanly now, and noticed that he still didn't know whether the essay would matter next month, whether seven levels could survive one bad week of exams. He put the phone face-down on his desk, and it buzzed once more before he let it go.

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Countering is when one actor shifts position to balance the stage after another actor crosses, keeping both visible to the audience.
story:
Parker had been appointed director of the winter one-act by a process he still could not describe to anyone without embarrassment. Ms. Horváth had taped a sign-up sheet to the door of the community theatre's green room, and when the smoke cleared he was the only name on the director line. The cast was not the problem. He had Esteban and Marek, both of whom could act, and a girl from the eleventh grade who could act better than both of them combined. The problem was the stage, which was small and shallow and seemed to have been designed by someone who disliked actors personally.

The first rehearsal established the terms of the difficulty. Marek played the brother who arrives unannounced, and his entrance required him to cross the stage repeatedly while Esteban, who played the brother who never left, stood more or less where he had been told to stand. Every time Marek walked past, Esteban vanished. Not literally. He simply ended up behind Marek's shoulder, in that dead zone downstage left where the audience could hear him but not see him, so that the scene played like a radio drama with occasional visual interruptions.

"You did it again," Esteban said, on the fourth or fifth occurrence. He did not sound angry, which was somehow worse. He sounded like a man compiling a file.

"I walked where the blocking says to walk," Marek said, holding up his binder like a small constitution. Parker had written the blocking himself, two nights earlier, at his kitchen table, with a diagram that had seemed at the time very authoritative. Now he saw that the diagram was essentially a fantasy. He had drawn positions without ever once imagining the transitions between them, which was, he was beginning to understand, like choreographing a dance while forgetting that people have bodies.

He told them to run it again and watched from the house, the empty rows of folding chairs presaging an audience that would see exactly what he was seeing: nothing. A stage that went blank whenever anyone moved. His father had offered some advice over dinner, something about leadership being a matter of confidence, and Parker had nodded while privately concluding that the advice was specious, confident nonsense delivered with the authority of a man who had never directed anything except traffic out of a driveway.

At the next rehearsal the girl from eleventh grade, whose name was on the cast list but whom everyone called by her character's name even offstage, stopped mid-scene. "When he crosses," she said, "I always move a little. Like a counterweight." She demonstrated, drifting half a step downstage as Marek passed her, and suddenly both of them were visible, balanced, the stage evenly weighted instead of collapsing into one corner. Parker stood up from his chair.

"Is that a thing?" he said. "Does that have a name?"

"Countering," she said, with a shrug that suggested the answer had cost her nothing. "My mom did community theatre."

He wrote it in the margin of his diagram, where it looked small for something that solved half his problems. Countering: when one actor crosses, another shifts to balance the stage so both stay visible to the audience. The rule of it pleased him, the way physics problems used to please him, cause and correction, an elegant little system. He drilled it that whole rehearsal. Marek crossed, Esteban countered; Marek crossed, the girl countered; the stage stopped going blind. By the end of the night they could do it without looking, and Parker walked home feeling like an engineer.

The feeling lasted until Thursday, when the trouble began, and the trouble was Marek. Marek had grasped the principle and then extended it, as Marek extended everything, into a private empire. He began countering other people's counters, adjusting his position whenever anyone breathed, and because he was the loudest personality in the cast, the others started deferring to his instincts over Parker's notes. By the end of the week Parker was standing in the wings watching three actors negotiate the stage among themselves while the director of record took notes nobody asked for. The production had become, in effect if not in name, an oligarchy of Marek, with a supporting regime of whoever happened to agree with him that evening.

He could have gone to Ms. Horváth, who arrived early on Saturdays to paint flats and whose presence generally restored order the way a thunderstorm restores weather. Instead he called Esteban that night, and they talked for forty minutes about what the play actually needed, which was not Marek's instinct or Parker's diagram but something between them: a set of rules everyone agreed to, plus the humility to break them when the scene demanded it. Parker admitted, out loud, that he did not entirely know where the line was between directing and just being the person whose name was on a sign-up sheet. Esteban said that was probably a good sign, or at least not a bad one, and then asked whether Parker thought Marek would take it well. Neither of them answered that.

At Saturday's run-through, Parker gathered the cast in the centre of the stage and made his case in about ninety seconds, shorter than anything he had prepared. Rules when they help, instincts when they don't, countering included, Marek's excesses excluded. Marek listened with his arms crossed, then uncrossed them, and said, "Fine, but then stop hiding me behind the doorframe on my entrance." Parker looked at the doorway, and at the blocking he had written, and at the diagram still folded in his back pocket. Marek was right. The entrance Parker was proudest of, the one he had drawn first, had been hiding his best actor for a week. "From the stairs instead," Parker said, and reached for his pencil.

activity: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
knowledge_domain: to plan a weekly training program for a sport with rest days and warm-ups
fact: Delayed-onset muscle soreness usually peaks 24 to 72 hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout, not right after it.
story:
The clipboard was Avery's idea, because a plan you could hold was harder to argue with than a plan you kept in your head. She had ruled the park's concrete picnic table into seven columns with a pencil, one for each day of the week, and at the top she had written the word REST in two of the columns and underlined it twice. The tryout for the county cross-country development squad was in eleven days, and between now and then she intended to become, in Mr. Friedman's phrase, someone the selectors noticed.

"Thursday and Sunday," she said to Lyndon, tapping the underlined words. "No running at all. Warm-up jog and drills before everything else, twenty minutes minimum." Lyndon sat across from her peeling an orange in one long spiral, which he could do and which she privately envied. It was early May, the grass still bright with the last of the morning watering, and the sprinklers at the far end of the park were ticking through their arcs with a patience she wanted to borrow.

"A rest day is a penurious use of eleven days," Lyndon said. He held up the spiral of peel to the light. "You have ten days to get better and you're spending two of them doing nothing."

"It's not nothing," Avery said. "That's the whole point of a plan." She didn't entirely believe this yet. The plan was, if she was honest, a way of reifying a hope, of turning wanting into a schedule with boxes she could tick, and she knew the difference between a hope and a schedule was not the same as the difference between wanting and having. But the boxes helped.

The first session went into the Tuesday column. She ran the park's outer loop four times with Aidan, who had made the squad last year and ran with his elbows close to his ribs like a man guarding a secret. The warm-up drills felt absurd, high knees and walking lunges by the playground while a toddler watched her with frank interest. The run itself felt easy, almost suspiciously easy. She finished the fourth loop and found she wasn't even breathing hard, and on the walk home she let herself imagine the tryout in detail, the elastic number pinned to her vest.

Wednesday she wrote planned rest and ignored it. Wednesday she felt fine, better than fine, and rest days, she decided, were for people who had earned them through exhaustion, and she had not been exhausted, and so she ran the loop three more times, faster, without drills, because drills took time and time was the thing she was shortest of. Aidan wasn't there. The sprinklers were off and the grass had gone dull, and a man was filling the drinking fountain with a wrench and a look of permanent grievance.

Thursday morning she woke and could not walk down the stairs properly. Her thighs had seized overnight into something rigid and burning, and lowering herself onto the kitchen chair required the use of both armrests and a certain amount of dignity she did not have to spare. Her mother watched from the doorway with the particular stillness of a person assembling an I-told-you-so, but all she said was that there were eggs.

Avery limped to the park anyway, because the plan said warm-up jog, twenty minutes, and she was the sort of person who had written the plan and therefore had to be the sort of person who kept it. The warm-up jog turned out to be a warm-up hobble of perhaps forty metres before she stopped under the big plane tree by the tennis courts, breathing carefully through her nose. Mr. Friedman was there, returning tennis balls to a bucket with a cone he had apparently invented for the purpose. He looked at her legs, then at her face, and said nothing for a while, which was his way of asking a question.

"I felt fine on Tuesday," Avery said. "Fine on Wednesday morning too. I didn't think anything was wrong."

"Delayed-onset muscle soreness," Mr. Friedman said. He picked up another ball. "Peaks twenty-four to seventy-two hours after an unfamiliar or intense workout. Not right after it." He dropped the ball into the bucket with a soft thock. "How many days since the first hard session?"

"Two," she said, and the arithmetic assembled itself in her chest with a sick little click. Two days. Peak. She had read her own body's silence as evidence of safety, and her body had simply been running late with its report.

She sat on the bench by the courts and took out the clipboard, and for a long time she did nothing with it. The metaphysics of the thing bothered her more than the pain did: the plan had said rest, the plan had been right, and she had overruled it because in the moment the rest had felt like cowardice. She had trusted the feeling that arrived first over the fact that arrived later, and the fact had won, the way facts tended to, arriving on its own schedule regardless of hers. She could not yet say how she would tell the difference next time between a rest day she needed and a rest day she was hiding inside. She wrote that question at the bottom of the page, under a line, where questions went.

Aidan found her there an hour later, still limping but moving, walking the loop with Lyndon on either side of her like an honor guard for the injured. "Thursday," Aidan said, reading the upside-down clipboard as they passed the picnic table. "It says rest."

"It says rest," Avery agreed. She walked on, slow and deliberate, feeling out each step the way you'd feel out ice. At the drinking fountain the man with the wrench had finally gone, and the water ran cold over her wrist, and she drank with both hands.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In a 1974 study by Donald Dutton and Arthur Aron, men who had just crossed a frightening suspension bridge were more likely to call a female interviewer afterward than men who crossed a sturdy bridge.
story:
Kyle was not nervous, which he told himself twice while he waited by the rental counter, once when Belle's text said she was parking and once when the skate sizes ran out and he had to requisition a pair of men's nines from the back room, promising the cashier he would return them personally. He was not a nervous person. That was simply true, a lemma he had proven many times: he had given a class presentation on Wuthering Heights without his voice shaking, and he had once told a substitute teacher that the assignment was pointless. Nerves belonged to other people, to Remy, who got a virulent case of them before every swim meet.

Belle came through the doors with her hair still damp from a shower she had obviously rushed, and she said, "You skate better than me, right? Because I'm going to fall," and Kyle heard himself say, "We'll find out," which was a strange answer, and she laughed at it anyway, which felt like luck.

The rink was half empty on a Tuesday, the music older than both of them, the ice squeaking under every blade. Belle did fall, twice, both times grabbing his arm on the way down, and the second time he went down with her and they sat on the cold rubber mat at the boards laughing while an old man in a referee shirt glided past without comment. Then Kyle, showing off a crossover he had learned three winters ago, caught a rut in the ice and went into the boards hard enough that his helmetless head rang. He stood up fast so she wouldn't worry. His heart was going like a fist on a door.

She held the sleeve of his jacket while they lap-skated slowly, and he was aware of her hand, and of his heart still slamming, and he could not tell the two things apart. Was the pounding for her, or was it the boards, or was it both braided together so tightly that unbraiding was impossible? He liked the question, actually. He liked questions more than answers, which Remy said was a cop-out, but Remy said a lot of things.

At the snack bar, drinking hot chocolate that tasted mostly of powder, he texted Remy, who was home with a twisted ankle and therefore contractually available for consultation. "How do you know if you like someone or if you're just scared," he typed, and Remy called him instead of texting back, because Remy treated every exchange as a hearing.

"There's this study," Remy said, his voice tinny under the rink's PA. "Nineteen seventy-four. These two researchers, Dutton and Aron. Guys crossing a scary suspension bridge got approached by a female interviewer, and guys on a sturdy bridge got the same interview. The scary-bridge guys were more likely to call her afterward."

"Call her," Kyle repeated, and glanced at Belle, who was watching a four-year-old fall in a way that suggested she found it beautiful.

"The interviewer. Her number was on the survey. That's the whole thing. That's all I know. I don't know why." Remy paused. "So maybe your heart doesn't know why either. Maybe it just reports."

Kyle hung up and put the phone face-down on the counter, and Belle said, "Who was that," and he said, "Remy. Telling me about a bridge," and she said, "Okay," in the tone of someone deciding not to follow up, which was its own kind of kindness.

Here is what he did not tell her, and this is the part where he has to be honest, at least with himself: when he fell into the boards, he had been skating badly on purpose, slightly, just enough to look casual rather than showing off, because showing off had felt desperate. So the fall was partly manufactured, which meant the fear was partly manufactured, which meant, if Remy's bridge study applied, that some fraction of what he was feeling toward her was an artifact of his own staging. He had built the suspension bridge himself. Or he hadn't, and the rut was just a rut, and he was frightened and smitten in the ordinary accidental proportions of everyone who had ever lapped a rink on a Tuesday. There was no instrument for sorting it. He thought of asking her to fall down on purpose next to him, as a control condition, and almost laughed out loud at himself for wanting a control condition on a first date.

The lights came up for the last fifteen minutes, that strange zamboni-yellow glow, and Belle stood and offered him her hand to pull him up, which was backwards, which she seemed to realize halfway through, so they just held it, standing, her glove and his bare palm. His heart was doing exactly what it had been doing since the boards. Maybe more.

"So," she said, as the old ref unlocked the exit door and cold parking-lot air came through it. "There's a horror movie at the dollar theater Friday."

Kyle looked at their two shadows stretched long across the scuffed ice, and then at her.

activity: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
knowledge_domain: to temper chocolate so it sets shiny and snaps cleanly
