"But is that in the painting or is that in us?" Amelia asked. "That's the part I can't separate. The tears, the nails, the cracked column, those are things Kahlo put there. The discomfort is what happens when they work. If I call it symbolism, I'm dodging. If I call it affective response, I'm not analyzing. If I say the viewer bears some culpability just for looking, I've stopped writing about art and started writing a court case."

Molly had been quiet, tearing the rim off her cup in a slow spiral. "Maybe you don't have to separate them," she said. "Maybe the whole point is that you can't. The nails and the eyes are doing it together. The suffering makes you want to turn away, and the gaze makes that impossible, and the painting exists in exactly that gap. That could be your thesis. The discomfort is where the form and the meaning are the same thing."

Amelia read back over her own draft, the neat paragraphs about palette and vertical composition, and felt the familiar vertigo of watching a position she had defended for two days quietly collapse. She had been treating the analysis like a checklist, as if the painting were a machine that could be taken apart with the right labels. She looked again at the printout. The figure stood against the split landscape, the iron corset holding the broken column in place, the small tears moving down the cheeks in steady lines, and the eyes, which were not pleading or accusing or closed in privacy but simply, unbearably, open and level and waiting.

"Okay," she said, and drew a line through her first paragraph. Then through the second. Jane watched her do it with visible satisfaction, as though she had personally caused it.

"Good," Jane said. "Now will you turn it over while I eat?"

"In a minute." Amelia wrote at the top of a fresh page: the gaze as composition. Below it she wrote: what remains uncertain is whether the discomfort belongs to the painting or to me, and whether that distinction matters. Then she underlined nothing, closed the notebook, and turned the printout face down on the table, sliding it toward Jane.

"There," she said. "Now it can't watch you eat."

"It's still watching," Jane said, and bit into a chip.

activity: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
knowledge_domain: to use a geographic information system to overlay flood risk and housing on a city map
fact: A buffer in GIS draws a zone of a set distance around a feature, such as every area within 100 meters of a river.
story:
The map filled the whole screen of Grandfather's old laptop, and Owen had been staring at it so long that the river had started to look like a living thing, a pale vein threading through the east side of the city. His class project was due in nine days: overlay flood risk on housing data and write about what the pattern showed. He had the flood layer, a green wash of polygons that stopped at boundaries drawn by officials decades ago. He had the housing layer, each parcel a small square tinted by value. What he didn't have was any idea what to do next.

He had brought the laptop to the kitchen table because the guest room had no outlet that worked, and because Grandfather liked company, even the silent kind. Grandfather read his newspaper at the counter and offered nothing except coffee, which Owen accepted even though it tasted like it had been percolating since morning.

The problem had been sitting in his head since Thursday, when Lili had leaned over his shoulder in the lab and pointed at a cluster of houses on the river's bend, just past the edge of the green. "My aunt lives there," she had said. "Flooded twice in the last few years. And it's not in the zone. So your map says she's safe." She hadn't meant it as an accusation, but it landed like one. The official layer was the official layer; who was he to contradict it? And yet the houses were right there, close enough to the water that he could almost hear it from the map.

The next morning Lili had messaged him a screenshot from her own exploration of the software, a menu item she'd found and didn't understand. "Is this anything?" she'd written. Owen clicked through to it now, at the kitchen table, while Grandfather turned a page. The menu offered to draw a zone of a set distance around a chosen feature. He entered a distance, a hundred meters, selected the river, and hit run.

The laptop thought about it, and then a new shape bloomed over the map: a band following the river's every curve, every area within a hundred meters of the water, whether the officials had claimed it or not. Owen sat back. "A buffer," he said aloud, reading the word from the menu, because that was what the tool called itself.

"So that's a buffer," Lili said that afternoon, when she came over with her bike helmet still on and stood behind him at the counter, Grandfather having migrated to the porch with his paper. "Everywhere within a hundred meters of the river." She traced the band with her finger, not quite touching the screen, and Owen watched the new shape swallow her aunt's whole street. Dozens of parcels. Maybe a hundred. Low values, mostly, which he could now see clearly because the housing layer sat underneath, tinting through.

Here was where his thinking began to divide against itself, and he let it. If he ran the analysis with the buffer included, he was choosing to interpolate between what the officials measured and what residents actually experienced, filling a gap with a distance he had picked himself. A hundred meters was a guess wearing the costume of a number. If he excluded it, he was treating the official zone as complete, which felt almost tautological: the map would prove that only houses in the flood zone were at flood risk, because that was how he had drawn it. He said as much to Lili, and she pulled a stool over and said, "So maybe the honest version is both maps. The official one and yours, side by side, with the gap showing." She tapped the screen where the buffer's edge ran through a block of small blue squares, houses neither green nor safe.

Mr. Cardinal from next door knocked on the screen door around four, holding a trowel he'd borrowed a week ago, and stayed to look because Grandfather flagged him in and because Owen's screen was now the most interesting thing in the room. Owen explained the layers, the buffer, the houses. Mr. Cardinal, who had lived on the east side for forty years, studied the bend of the river and said, "Those streets took water in the spring of the big melt. Nobody redraws a line for a thing like that. The water just goes where it goes." Owen asked him which houses, and Mr. Cardinal set down the trowel and pointed with one thick finger, parcel by parcel, while Owen marked them, small red pins accumulating along the bend like a second kind of evidence.

By evening he had three things on the map: the official zone, the buffer, and Mr. Cardinal's memory. He didn't yet know how to weight them against one another, or whether weighting them was even a word that made sense here, and he suspected that uncertainty would follow the project all the way to its final paragraph. But he had learned something that felt sturdier than the conclusion he was supposed to reach, which was that a flood was not only water; it was also a decision someone once made about where the water was allowed to count, and a risk quietly handed to the people who lived just past that decision, an externality drawn in nobody's ledger. Lili texted him a photo of her aunt's porch with the caption "evidence." He pinned that too.

activity: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
knowledge_domain: to write a historiographical essay on how views of the French Revolution have changed since 1800
fact: Marxist historian Albert Soboul argued the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class.
story:
Rachel found the museum label on a Tuesday, on a class trip she had mostly treated as an excuse to miss chemistry. THE REVOLUTION OF 1789: A BOURGEOIS RISING AGAINST FEUDAL ORDER, it said, in the confident lowercase of someone paid to be certain. She copied it into her phone and kept walking, and it wasn't until she was on the bus home, watching Sarina sleep against the window, that she wondered whose sentence that actually was. Somebody wrote it. Somebody believed it. The label hadn't said.

The essay was due in three weeks, and Mr. González had assigned it with a warning. "Historiography," he said, writing the word on the board and then boxing it like a suspect, "is not what happened. It is what people decided happened, and why." He wanted them to trace how views of the French Revolution had shifted since 1800, and he had forbidden them to answer with a timeline of the Revolution itself. "If your essay is about Robespierre," he said, "you have failed. If it is about why historians argue about Robespierre, you are beginning."

She started in the school library after last bell, when the radiators ticked and the chairs scraped in that hollow way that made the room feel bigger than it was. Rohan was already there, surrounded by books he had pulled for a project on the Levant, and he watched her work through the section on France with something like pity. "You look like an ascetic," he said. "Like you've given up food and comfort for this."

"I've given up lunch," she said.

The first problem was that everything contradicted. A book from 1962 called the Revolution the triumph of a rising commercial class over a dying feudal order, and a book from 1990 called that same account a myth invented by academics who needed history to move in their direction. Rachel wrote both claims on separate index cards and stared at them as if a third card might materialize between them and arbitrate. Rohan leaned over and read them. "They can't both be right."

"Maybe they can both be honest," she said, and felt, immediately, that she had said something she didn't yet understand.

The name surfaced on Thursday, buried in a footnote smaller than the rest of the text, as though the typesetter had been embarrassed by it: Soboul. She followed the citation to a thick volume shelved at the wrong height for comfort, and stood in the aisle reading until her arms ached. Albert Soboul, a Marxist historian, had argued that the Revolution was the moment the bourgeoisie overthrew feudal society and became the dominant class. She read the sentence twice. It was the museum label, word for word in spirit, a decade older and with a body of argument behind it. Someone had stood at a display case in her city, forty years later, and turned Soboul's thesis into plain institutional fact, unattributed, like weather. That was what made her uneasy, though it took her the walk home to name it: not the claim itself, but the laundering of it, the way an argument had been dressed up as information.

"Whose interpretation is that?" she asked Mr. González the next morning, showing him the photo of the label.

He looked at it for a long moment, and she braced for a lecture, but he only handed the phone back. "That's your essay," he said. "Not the answer. The question."

She went home and did not write. She made tea she didn't drink and sat with the cards spread on the kitchen table while her mother asked from the hallway whether she was all right. The Marxist account had its elegance: the Revolution as something tectonic, a slow collision of classes rather than a drama of individuals, and the elegance was exactly what made it persuasive and exactly what made her suspicious, because the world she lived in was not elegant, and the 1990 historian had gone through Soboul's account sentence by sentence and found the bourgeoisie thinner on the ground than the theory required. She had, by now, four cards that leaned toward Soboul and three that leaned against, and one card, unlabeled, on which she had written only: labels.

On Monday she went back to Rohan, who was still on the Levant and pontificating about it to anyone who sat down. "You said they can't both be right," she said. "I've been stuck on that for a week."

"I was making conversation," Rohan said. "I don't actually know anything about France."

"I think that's the point," Rachel said. "Neither does the museum. Not really. It knows what somebody told it." She laid out the cards, Soboul's claim beside its critics, and moved them around like a hand of cards she was deciding whether to play. "So the essay isn't me picking a side. It's me saying: here is where the argument came from, here is what it explained well, here is where it broke, and here is what still isn't settled. Because it isn't settled. I checked. People are still fighting about it in journals nobody reads."

Sarina, who had drifted over and heard the last part, frowned at the cards. "But you'll lose marks for not concluding anything."

"Maybe," Rachel said. She gathered the cards, squared them, and slid them into the front pocket of her binder, where she could feel their edge against her palm when she picked it up.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, the horizontal distance a projectile travels equals its constant horizontal velocity multiplied by its time in the air.
story:
The marble launcher had three settings, and I had already decided which one I would use before I touched it, which was probably my first mistake, though at the time I thought of it as efficiency. Ms. Clarke-Williams wanted us to predict where the marble would land, on paper, before we fired a single shot. Rachelle said that defeated the purpose of an experiment; I said that was exactly the point of an experiment, and neither of us conceded anything, which is how we usually work.

Alistair had finished his calculations in four minutes and then spent twenty narrating them to anyone in range. I want to say nobody listened, but the truth is I listened more than I admitted, because he kept saying the same phrase over and over: "time in the air." He would enunciate it, both words, as though the marble deserved to hear it clearly. Half the class thought he was brilliant. The other half thought he was a sycophant with a calculator, and I had put myself in that second half mostly because it was easier than doing the work.

The problem on the sheet was simple to state. A marble leaves the launcher at a known speed and a known angle, and a target sits some distance away along the floor. The vertical and horizontal motions refuse to be solved together in any way I could manage; the angle made a diagonal of the velocity, and the diagonal kept swallowing my numbers whole. I had two columns on my page, and I believed they were enemies.

I asked Ms. Clarke-Williams nothing, which I want you to notice, because later I told Rachelle I had asked plenty of questions and she looked at me like I was describing someone else. What I actually did was divide the diagonal into a vertical part and a horizontal part using the angle, and then, on an impulse I can't fully account for, I wrote the vertical part at the top of the left column and the horizontal part at the top of the right column and pretended they had never met. Two strangers. Two separate lives.

The left column went beautifully. Up and down, decelerating, a height, a time. The marble would stay in the air a little under half a second, and that number felt solid in a way the others hadn't, like a coin on a table. Then I sat there with half a second in my hand and nowhere to put it, and Alistair drifted past my station, and I heard him say, almost to himself, "Time in the air," and I looked at the right column and thought, well, what has the horizontal half of the marble been doing all that time?

Nothing but traveling, I decided. Sideways, evenly, unbothered. So I took the horizontal velocity, constant for as long as the marble flew, and multiplied it by the time in the air, and out came a distance. I remember the specific sensation, which was suspicion. It couldn't be that the landing point was just one multiplication away, that everyone who had ever found the flight time was holding the answer and didn't know it. I checked it twice. I checked it a third time in a different order, as though the numbers might object to being asked in the wrong sequence.

Rachelle leaned over. "You look like you found money."

"I found where it lands." I showed her the two columns. "Vertical tells me how long. Horizontal tells me how far, per second. Multiply." She frowned at it, and I watched her distrust it the way I had, and I understood that the distrust was part of the thing, not an obstacle to it. Somewhere in there I also understood something about Alistair, or thought I did, though I've been wrong about him before and might be again. Maybe he wasn't performing. Maybe he was just saying aloud what he was amazed by.

We put the target where the multiplication said. Ms. Clarke-Williams walked the room checking predictions, prolix as ever in her margins, and when she reached our station she only tapped the right column twice and moved on, which from her is a parade. Then I set the launcher to the setting I had already chosen, the one I had been sure of since the beginning, and Rachelle knelt down by the target with the tape measure, and I said, "Ready," and pressed the release.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier.
story:
The camp stove had two burners and one temperamental knob, and Rachel had claimed both before anyone else woke. Her parents were still in the tent, her little brother asleep in the car with his mouth open, and the morning air smelled of cold ash and pine. On the picnic table sat a bag of flour, a jar of salt, a packet of yeast she had smuggled past her mother's grocery inspection, and a dented pot for dough. She was going to make bread. Real bread, in the woods, on a camp stove, because her grandmother had done it once and Rachel had decided, somewhere on the long drive up, that she was the kind of person who could do it too.

The first loaf, yesterday, had been a disaster. Dense as a hockey puck, crumbly where it should have torn soft, tasting of yeast and regret. Her brother had eaten two slices anyway, dunking them in cocoa so they would soften enough to chew. Rachel had lain awake in the tent replaying the afternoon. She had mixed flour and water and yeast, waited for the dough to rise, shaped it, baked it in the battered camping oven Mr. Ferreira had lent them from the site next door. Every step had felt like following a map drawn from memory. Somewhere she had gone wrong, and she suspected she knew where, but she wanted to be sure before she wasted another bag of flour.

"You're up early," said a voice from the trail. It was Jaeden, from the site across the road, carrying his own bag of flour in a way that suggested it was not entirely his idea. He had announced himself the first night by walking over to ask if they had a corkscrew, then stayed for an hour talking about a bread competition his older sister had won two summers ago. Jaeden wanted to beat her this year, at the county fair in August. He had said so twice, casually, the way people mention things they care about too much.

"My second attempt," Rachel said, nodding at the table. "The first one came out like a brick."

"Did you knead it?" Jaeden set his flour down and poked at her dough-in-progress with one finger, a doctor assessing a patient. "My sister says that's where everyone fails. Gluten forms when the wheat proteins glutenin and gliadin mix with water, and kneading longer makes the gluten network stronger and the bread chewier." He shrugged, as if disclaiming ownership of the knowledge. "Her words. I just know my first loaves were crumbly and hers weren't."

Rachel looked at her own hands, already dusted white. Yesterday she had kneaded for maybe three minutes, impatient with the stickiness, wanting the dough to behave before it had any reason to. The crumbly, dense loaf suddenly made a kind of sense, and she felt both relieved and slightly annoyed: the answer had been available all along, and she had quit too soon. She poured more water into the bowl, worked it through, and started again, this time pushing the dough with the heel of her hand, folding it, turning it, pushing again.

A memory surfaced, unbidden. Two summers ago, at her grandmother's kitchen table, flour everywhere, the radio on. Her grandmother had kneaded without hurry, and Rachel, sixteen years younger and infinitely more restless, had asked why she kept going when the dough already looked smooth. "It's not done when it looks done," her grandmother had said, which at the time Rachel had filed under old-people riddles. Now she turned the dough over and kept pushing, and understood the sentence differently, though she wasn't sure she understood it completely even now. Some things only looked done. Some things, like her grandmother's patience, had been a practice rather than a mood, and Rachel had mistaken it for a temperament she simply hadn't inherited.

By the time her mother emerged from the tent in her spartan camping uniform of fleece and rubber sandals, the dough had been kneading for a solid ten minutes and had gone from shaggy to elastic to something that stretched under Rachel's fingers like it had opinions. Jaeden watched from the bench, taking notes on his phone for the fair. Alison arrived from the showers with wet hair, looked at the table, and said, "You're doing this again? Voluntarily?"

"I subjugated the first loaf," Rachel said. "It lost. This one gets a fair fight." Alison laughed, sat down, and stole a pinch of dough to taste, which Rachel allowed only because Alison had brought coffee.

The dough rose in the sun-warmed pot, and while it rose, Mr. Ferreira wandered over to reclaim a spatula and stayed to watch. He didn't offer advice, which Rachel appreciated. He had run this campground for thirty years, he'd said, and had learned that people who borrowed his oven generally wanted to be left alone with their failures. He sat in his folding chair with the contentment of a man with nowhere better to be, and when Rachel punched the dough down and felt it spring back under her fist, he raised his mug to her.

The loaf came out of the camp oven golden and hollow-sounding when she tapped its base. She tore it open while it was still too hot, the way her grandmother used to, and the inside stretched in strings instead of crumbling into sand. Chewy. Properly, stubbornly chewy. Her brother ate four slices. Her mother closed her eyes over hers, which in her family was the highest available praise. Jaeden asked for the exact times, the ratios, wrote everything down twice, and said, "In August, when I win, I'll mention you in the speech." Rachel said he could mention her or not, she hadn't decided whether she wanted credit for a win or distance from a loss.

That night, lying in the tent with the fire dying outside, Rachel found she was thinking about her grandmother's loaf from two summers ago, the one she had watched without really seeing. There was no way to know whether this morning's bread would have passed that older, stricter judgment, whether three more minutes of kneading yesterday, or ten fewer today, would have tipped it one way or the other. She had a hypothesis and one good loaf, which was not the same as knowing. Alison's voice came through the nylon, low, asking if there would be bread again tomorrow. Rachel looked at the dark square of the tent ceiling and said, "Bring the coffee and find out."

activity: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
knowledge_domain: to explain comparative advantage and why two countries both gain from trading
fact: David Ricardo set out comparative advantage in his 1817 book On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation, using England and Portugal trading cloth and wine.
story:
The Saturday market opened at seven, and by seven fifteen Elijah had already miscounted a customer's change twice. He was working the coffee and pastry stall for Mr. Becker, who had hired him three weekends ago, and who had noticed the textbook wedged beside the cash box before Elijah had even tied his apron.

"Exam Monday?" Mr. Becker asked, not unkindly.

"Economics. There's this one thing I can't keep straight." Elijah slid a croissant into a paper sleeve. "Comparative advantage. Everyone keeps telling me it's simple and then making it sound like a riddle."

By ten the rush thinned and the market went quiescent, just the hum of coolers and a bee exploring the honey stall next door. That was when Kenza appeared, canvas bag over her shoulder, and dropped two apples on the counter as if they were payment for his attention.

"I have the same exam," she said. "I've been quizzing myself while I shop. Portugal and England."

Elijah wiped his hands on his apron. "Wait. Which one did the wine?"

"You tell me."

He closed his eyes and tried to picture the page. His father had a way of talking about this stuff at dinner, how whole countries were like people who should specialize and trade, and it had always sounded to Elijah like a kind of arithmetic kindness, everyone winning at once. But the page kept sliding. "Portugal did wine," he said slowly. "England did cloth. It was in some book from way back. Ricardo, maybe?"

"Ricardo," Kenza agreed. "1817, On the Principles of Political Economy and Taxation. Xavier made me memorize the whole title like it was a spell."

Elijah laughed, and Mr. Becker, restacking cups, laughed too. "Xavier still buying the sourdough he can't afford?"

"He says he's a connoisseur," Kenza said. "He says knowing what's good is its own kind of wealth."

"Connoisseurs," Mr. Becker said, "are why I sell half my croissants to people who come back Sunday for more."

It was Xavier himself, in fact, who ambled up twenty minutes later with hisReusable bag and his opinions. When Kenca told him Elijah was still shaky on the idea, Xavier planted his elbows on the counter. "Look, my uncle has two shops. One fixes phones, one fixes watches. He's better than his cousin at both. But he sends all the watches to the cousin anyway."

"Why," Elijah said, "if he's better?"

"Because every hour he spends on watches is an hour not spent on phones, and that's where the gap is biggest. That's the whole thing. Two people, two goods, both gain by trading anyway." Xavier bit into a sample cookie with great ceremony. "Your dad never explained this to you?"

"He explained it like a speech. It doesn't operationalize for me until I have to use it on something real." Elijah frowned at the espresso machine as if it were a small country. "Okay, so England, cloth. Portugal, wine. Both still gain. I can hold that now."

"There's a question on the practice exam," Kenza said, quieter. "It asks whether the theory holds if one country is better at everything, like really better, by a lot. I wrote that it does, and then I sat there wondering if that's actually fair, or just efficient."

The three of them stood with that for a moment. Elijah thought of his father again, the way he'd said trade makes everyone better off, and how his mother, who had lost her job the year the plant moved, had left the table without answering. Both of those things were in him now, and he couldn't make them into one clean sentence.

"I'll write the theory down properly," Elijah said finally. "And then, if there's room, I'll write that it says nothing about who gets to keep the gains, or for how long. That part's still an argument."

"That'll cost you marks," Xavier said.

"Maybe. Or maybe the marker's tired of riddles too."

Mr. Becker rang up a coffee for a woman with a stroller, and the market noise picked up again around them, vendors calling prices, someone sampling cheese. Kenza took her apples. Xavier took his sourdough, and counted out coins that were mostly nickels.

"Monday," Kenza said, walking backward into the crowd. "Portugal and wine. England and cloth. Don't mix them up."

"I won't," Elijah called, and realized he believed it, and that believing it settled almost nothing else. He turned back to the counter and started the next order of croissants.

activity: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
knowledge_domain: to compute the electric field strength at a point between two charged plates
fact: The electric field between charged plates points from the positive plate toward the negative plate, the direction a positive charge would be pushed.
story:
The garage smelled of motor oil and the lemon tea Lewis's mother always left out for them, and Hannah had forty minutes before Ms. Sánchez collected the problem set at the start of first period. She sat on an overturned milk crate with her notebook on her knees, because the folding chair had been claimed by Ali, who was using it as a desk for a diagram of two charged plates drawn with what Hannah could only call misplaced confidence.

"Read it to me again," Hannah said. "The actual words on the page."

"Two large parallel plates carry equal and opposite charges," Ali read, holding the worksheet at arm's length as though distance would improve it. "Compute the field strength at point P, midway between them." She tapped her diagram. "So the top plate is positive, I've decided, and I've drawn the arrows going up, from negative toward positive, because it looked nicer that way."

"It did look nicer," Lewis admitted from the workbench, where he was supposed to be tightening something on his bike and was in fact watching them like a man at a tennis match. "Very symmetrical. Very wrong, possibly. Which is it?"

Hannah bent over the diagram. The plates were drawn as clean horizontal lines, the arrows a tidy row of little flagpoles pointing skyward, and at the midpoint sat point P, circled twice, obdurate in its smallness. She wanted the arrows to be right, because if they were right, the problem was ten minutes of arithmetic and she could still drink her tea while it was warm. If they were wrong, she had to know which way they actually pointed, and she had never quite trusted herself on that.

"Think about a proton," she said slowly. "If you dropped a positive charge between the plates, which way would it go?"

"Does that matter?" Ali said.

"It has to matter. It's the only thing in here I can picture." Hannah drew a tiny plus sign floating at point P, a little balloon of a charge, and tried to imagine it choosing. "The positive plate would push it away, because they're both positive, they'd hate each other. The negative plate would pull it, because opposites attract. So the push and the pull agree. The proton gets shoved from the positive plate toward the negative one." She looked up. "The field points the way a positive charge would be pushed. From positive to negative. That's the rule, or it's the rule I actually believe."

Lewis set down his wrench. "So you're saying her arrows are backwards."

"I'm saying the arrows point from the positive plate toward the negative plate," Hannah said, "and hers point the other way." She took the pen out of Ali's hand, flipped the top plate's label, and redrew the row of arrows pointing down, toward the negative plate at the bottom. Ali made a small wounded noise, like a cat denied a windowsill.

"You could have just said the field points from positive to negative," Ali said. "You didn't have to perform it."

"The performing is how I remember it," Hannah said. "If I transliterate it into proton language, it sticks. Proton goes down. Field goes down. Forever."

"That is not what transliterate means," Lewis said.

"It means carrying something across from one language into another, and I am carrying it from physics into a tiny imaginary balloon, so yes it does," Hannah said, and Ali laughed so hard she nearly knocked the tea off the crate. Hannah copied the corrected diagram into her own notebook, did the arithmetic twice because she did not trust herself under deadline, and got the same number both times, which she chose to find reassuring rather than suspicious.

"Admit it, though," Ali said, collecting the worksheets into a neat stack as the garage door rattled in the wind. "You didn't know that rule with certainty twenty minutes ago. You just talked yourself into it."

"I knew it," Hannah said. "I didn't trust that I knew it. Those are different." She zipped her bag and checked the time on the microwave clock through the door to the kitchen. Twenty-two minutes. "Whether I'm right about the proton's opinion of the positive plate, we find out at first period, and if I'm wrong, I'm blaming your flagpole arrows."

"I'd respect you more as an autodidact if you took responsibility for your own balloons," Lewis said, and held the garage door open for both of them, bike forgotten, wrench still lying on the bench where he'd left it.

activity: applying to college and waiting for the answer
knowledge_domain: applying to college and waiting for the answer
fact: Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open.
story:
The portal loaded at 6:58, two minutes before the hour it had promised, and Cameron sat with his hands flat on the desk so they wouldn't drift to the trackpad. The first line said thank you for your application. The second line said waitlist. He read it three times, then opened a new tab and looked up the deposit deadline for Alder University, the school he could actually attend, the one with the good engineering program and the financial aid letter already printed and taped above his monitor. May 1. He went back to the waitlist letter and found, near the bottom, a sentence about when spots might open. Many US colleges fill waitlist spots in May, after admitted students have sent deposits and the college knows how many places are still open. He read that three times too, and then he did the only thing that seemed reasonable, which was to text Rayan.

"Waitlisted at Fairview," he typed. "Alder deposit due May 1. What do I even do."

Rayan called instead of texting back. "Dude, that's basically an acceptance with a delay," Rayan said, his voice doing the optimistic thing it always did, the thing Cameron had slowly become inured to and depended on anyway. "You just wait. They said May, right? May is right after the deposit thing. So you wait like three weeks."

"That's the problem. I have to pay Alder first. Three hundred dollars. If Fairview takes me off the waitlist in May, I lose the money. If I don't pay Alder and Fairview says no, I have nowhere to go."

There was a pause on the line long enough that Cameron could hear Rayan's television in the background, someone scoring something. "Okay, so pay Alder," Rayan said. "Three hundred is the price of not being homeless in September."

Cameron looked at the printed aid letter above his monitor, at the number his mother had circled twice in pencil, and didn't answer. After they hung up he opened the Fairview portal again, as if the sentence might have changed, and then he opened his essay file, the one about his grandfather's toolbox, which he had revised eleven times and which had apparently gotten him exactly as far as maybe.

Flavie came over the next evening, which she did most Thursdays, carrying the specific groceries she liked and planning to cook them in his kitchen while he watched. He told her while she was chopping an onion, because her hands were busy and she couldn't gesture at him. He explained the waitlist, explained the deposits, explained May, explained the three hundred dollars. She set the knife down anyway.

"So you're saying the schools find out how many spots they have left only after everyone's paid everywhere," she said. "Which means the whole system runs on people like you paying for a maybe."

"Basically."

"Then pay Alder," she said. "You know I'd say the opposite if it was your dream school and it was free. But you told me in October that Fairview was a reach you applied to because your counselor said apply to reaches. Alder is the school you actually visited twice."

He wanted to argue and found he mostly agreed, which was worse. "It's not about which one I like," he said. "It's that I don't like deciding by paying for both options. That feels like the decision making itself."

Flavie picked the knife back up. "Then decide before you pay," she said. "Decide like Alder is it. Genuinely. And if Fairview calls in May, you get to decide again, and that one will be free."

Here is what Flavie did not say, because she had decided long ago that saying it would be a kind of interference she had no right to. She had watched Cameron revise that essay eleven times, and she had watched him tape the Alder letter above his monitor, which was a strange thing to do for a safety school. Her own acceptance had come in March, unremarkable, to a program she had chosen mostly because it was far from her mother's apartment, and she suspected that her whole college plan was a series of reasonable-sounding exits rather than an entrance. She thought Cameron was doing something braver than she was, holding two futures open at once, and she thought the three hundred dollars was not really the problem. The problem was that choosing meant becoming one person instead of every person he might have been, and eighteen was early for that, and also it was time.

On Saturday his mother found him at the computer again, the Fairview portal open in one tab, Alder's payment page in another. She stood behind him with a dish towel over her shoulder and read both screens.

"Ms. Wright came by," she said. "She asked about your news. I told her waitlist. She said her niece waited three weeks one year, and the call came the second week of May, after the deposits were all counted. And the niece went. Happily."

"That's one niece," Cameron said. "That's not odds. That's a family story."

"So pay Alder, and if the call comes, we'll figure the three hundred out." She put a hand on his shoulder, brief, somatic in a way no advice could be, and he felt the weight of it in his chest before he felt it as pressure on bone. "Or don't. But choose something by May 1, because the waiting is eating you. I can see it in how you sit."

He pulled his wallet from the desk drawer, took out the card, and held it without typing anything. His body had an injunction of its own, some old instruction that said money in hand is safety, money spent is gone. His grandfather had carried it through two recessions and then, at the end, spent almost nothing at all. Cameron set the card on the keyboard and looked at the Alder payment page, the little empty boxes, the total at the bottom, the word submit doing more work than any word that small should have to.

He typed the card number. He stopped before the expiration date. Outside, a neighbor's kid was drawing on the driveway with chalk, an enormous sun with too many rays, the kind of drawing that commits to nothing except brightness. Cameron picked up his phone instead, opened the thread with Rayan, and typed, "If I pay Alder tonight, does that mean I've decided, or just that I've paid?"

Rayan's reply took four minutes, which for Rayan was geological. It said, "Come over and find out."

activity: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
knowledge_domain: to plan a week of meals, shop for the ingredients and cook them in batches
fact: The shelf label's unit price shows the cost per gram, litre or item, which lets shoppers compare packages of different sizes fairly.
story:
His mother's note on the fridge read like a dare: five dinners, one shopping trip, one Sunday afternoon of cooking, and then she and his father would be away until Friday. Oliver had agreed too quickly, the way he agreed to things at the kitchen table, and now it was Saturday morning and the dare was his. He sat with a legal pad and tried to imagine a week. He wanted it to be orderly, thrugal, almost architectural: a pot of chili that would become two nights, a tray of roast vegetables, a soup that improved by Thursday. He had watched his mother do this for years without ever once doing it himself, and he understood now that watching was not the same as knowing, the way he had watched Derrick solve calculus problems all semester and then failed the exam alone.

The plan took two hours and three drafts. On the fourth draft he wrote quantities beside each meal, then added them up into a list, then crossed out half the list because the total at the bottom of the pad frightened him. His father came through the kitchen, looked over his shoulder, and said nothing, which Oliver chose to take as respect rather than doubt, though he was not certain which it was.

At the store he pushed the cart like a man with a mission, and for a while it was exhilarating, choosing the onions, weighing the sweet potatoes in his hand, being the one who decided. In the cereal aisle he stopped at the oats. He needed a kilogram, maybe more, because oats were cheap and filling and appeared twice in his plan. There was a large bag, nearly two kilograms, and a smaller one beside it. He reached for the large bag first, on an instinct so deep it felt like arithmetic: big meant cheaper, always had, his whole life.

Then he saw the small print on the shelf label. Below the price of each bag there was a second figure, smaller and unglamorous, and above it the words unit price. He looked closer. The label showed the cost per gram for each package, laid out plainly, as if it had been waiting there all along. He read the two numbers twice. The big bag cost more per gram than the small one. He stood in the aisle holding both bags, feeling something rearrange. The store, it turned out, was not a place of honest sizes; it was a place where packaging made arguments, and the shelf label was the only thing that spoke without trying to persuade him. He put the big bag back. At the rice, he checked again, and there the large bag did win, and he bought it, and the checking itself began to feel like a private competence, small but real.

In the next aisle he found Kareem, who worked Saturdays restocking, stacking cans with the obdurate patience of someone who had decided the job was beneath him and would do it perfectly anyway. "You look intense," Kareem said. "Unit price," Oliver said, pointing at the label. Kareem glanced at it and shrugged. "People never read that." Oliver thought about telling him it should be printed in bold, taught in school, lionized the way people lionized whoever had invented coupons, but instead he just said, "The big oats weren't cheaper," and Kareem laughed and said that was the oldest trick in the store, and went back to his cans.

Sunday he cooked. The chili scorched slightly on the bottom because he had left it to answer a text, and he stood over the pot remembering that, weighing whether to stir the burnt layer in or ladle around it. He ladled around it. He had read that chili forgiven is chili improved, and he wanted that to be true, though he could not verify it until Wednesday. He roasted the vegetables, cooked a pot of rice, portioned everything into containers with masking-tape labels, and by evening the fridge looked like a plan made solid, which, he supposed, was exactly what it was.

By Wednesday the chili was better and the soup was thinner than he had hoped. He ate alone at the counter, texting Derrick a photograph of the containers, and Derrick replied with a thumbs up and the word dad, which Oliver chose not to interpret. He had spent less than the pad's frightening total, and he knew now that this was partly cleverness and partly luck, and he could not fully separate the two. The unit price had saved him maybe two dollars. The planning had saved more, or maybe it had only changed where the money went.

When his parents came home Friday, there were two containers left, and his mother stood with the fridge door open, reading the tape labels the way he had read the shelf labels, and he waited to see whether she would ask how, or why, or say nothing again. She took out the soup, tasted it from the container, and said, "You used the good paprika." He said that he had. What stayed uncertain, what he turned over while she heated the soup, was whether a week counted as learning to do something or only as having done it once, and whether the difference mattered, and he was still holding both questions when she set two bowls on the table and told him to sit down.

activity: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
knowledge_domain: to compose a sixteen-bar melody with chord changes and write it in standard notation
fact: A half cadence ends a phrase on the V chord, which sounds unfinished and makes the listener expect another phrase to follow.
story:
The music room smelled like valve oil and old radiators, and Kaitlyn had filled her manuscript paper with crosses, arrows, and one small drawing of a duck wearing a crown, which was the honest portrait of how her melody was going. Sixteen bars, with chord changes, written in real notation, due Friday. She had eight bars that worked and eight that sounded like a xylophone falling down a staircase, and the deadline sat in her planner like a smug little bank.

"Stop agonizing," said Tatiana, who was supposed to be practicing scales and was instead lying across two chairs with her phone above her face. "Agonizing is last year's zeitgeist. This year we simply decide things and move on." Tatiana could proselytize about anything, from the superiority of minor keys to the correct way to peel an orange, and she delivered every opinion with the serene confidence of someone who had never once checked a fact.

Aaliyah, at the piano, actually practiced. She played Kaitlyn's eight finished bars straight through, and even the duck-crown bars sounded better under Aaliyah's hands, which was both kind and mildly insulting. When she reached the last note of bar eight, though, she stopped and stared at the page.

"What?"

"Nothing. Play it again," Aaliyah said, and played it again, and stopped again at the same spot, and then laughed. "It's like when you're telling a story and you stop to drink water. I keep waiting for more. Why does it do that?"

Kaitlyn leaned over her own paper. The chords underneath bars one through seven had mostly settled where they wanted to settle, but at the end of bar eight she had written a chord that never arrived home, that left the whole phrase standing in a doorway. She played it herself. Her left hand hung in the air afterward like it was waiting for a bus. "I didn't do that on purpose," she admitted. "I think I just couldn't decide where to land."

Ms. Chea drifted past on her circuit of the room, glancing at manuscripts, saying things like "lovely" and "count that again." She looked at Kaitlyn's page for exactly four seconds. "Nice eighth bar," she said, and moved on, which was the pedagogical equivalent of a wink, and Kaitlyn found this deeply suspicious.

"Go ask her," Tatiana commanded from the chairs.

"No. Then it's her idea." Kaitlyn pulled out the worn theory workbook from the shelf by the metronomes and flipped until she found the diagrams of phrase endings, the ones with brackets and arrows she'd skipped back in September. There it was, bar eight circled in the book's example, the same shape as hers: a phrase that ends on the five chord. The book had a name for it, and when she read the name out loud Aaliyah made her say it twice. "A half cadence," Kaitlyn repeated. "That's what it's called. It ends on the five chord, so it sounds unfinished, like the whole thing is just waiting for the next phrase." She sat back. "So I didn't mess up. I accidentally did a thing."

"So then write the next phrase," said Aaliyah, as if this were obvious, and of course it was obvious, and of course it was also the entire problem, because the reason her back eight bars were a disaster was that she'd been trying to start a new conversation instead of answering the one her front eight had started. She cleared the duck and the arrows, took a fresh sharpened pencil, and began again from bar nine, following the question her own melody had asked without her permission.

Tatiana appointed herself executive producer and offered chord suggestions, most of them terrible, one of them startlingly good. When Kaitlyn finally wrote the last note of bar sixteen, Aaliyah played the whole thing through, and at the end of bar eight Tatiana, who had sworn she wasn't even listening, said quietly, without opening her eyes, "Don't stop there."

"I'm not," Kaitlyn said. "Keep going."
